profile.address: Britton Parkway, Hilliard, Norwich Township, Franklin County, Ohio, 43026
profile.reading:
This entry sits within a cluster of Amazon Web Services data center campuses that AWS has built along a corridor of suburban business parks in Hilliard, Ohio, a western suburb of Columbus, as part of the AWS US East (Ohio) -- us-east-2 -- cloud region. The Britton Parkway address places this facility among at least three distinct campuses AWS has assembled in Hilliard since the mid-2010s: an original campus at 5109 Hayden Run Road, where construction began in 2015 and a third building was added in November 2019; a second campus of roughly 104 acres between Cosgray and Leppert roads, developed through land purchases from the City of Hilliard (about $11.76 million) and the Hilliard City School District (about $2.8 million) toward a project pegged at around $200 million when it was approved in 2021; and a third, newer campus on 142 acres off Scioto Darby Road, approved in 2022, whose land closing on New Year's Eve 2020 helped fund a city recreation complex known as The Well.

As with nearly all AWS facilities, Amazon does not publish square footage, IT capacity in megawatts, or cooling design for any single Hilliard building -- the company treats individual data center specifications as a competitive and security matter and instead speaks in aggregate about its Ohio region and broader US buildout. What is public is the friction the newest phase of that buildout has generated locally: to power the Scioto Darby campus, AEP Ohio proposed a 228-cell, six-acre fuel cell installation as a "bridge" power source ahead of new transmission capacity, a plan the Ohio Power Siting Board approved in September and the Ohio EPA issued an air permit for in October, over Hilliard officials' objections that state authority pre-empted local review. Residents near the site raised concerns about an estimated one million pounds of daily carbon dioxide emissions and the safety of a technology they consider unproven at this scale; the city has since appealed the EPA permit decision.

Whether this particular Britton Parkway building sits within the Hayden Run campus, the Cosgray/Leppert campus, or a separate parcel is not resolved by public sources at building-address granularity, but it is unambiguously part of the same expanding AWS Ohio footprint. It illustrates a pattern common to hyperscale cloud operators: enormous capital and power commitments disclosed at the campus or regional level, paired with near-total silence on any individual building's technical specifications, leaving local land records, utility filings, and permitting disputes as the main public window into what is actually being built.

Reused from operator-level research completed in an earlier phase of this project (twoai_dc_operators row: Amazon Web Services, operator-level status: complete).

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginias Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWSs own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginias position as AWSs most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone. This facility is recorded under the operator name Amazon Web Services us-east-2 datacenter in this registry, referring to part of the AWS us-east-2 (Ohio) region infrastructure operated by Amazon Web Services. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
Amazon does not publish the megawatt capacity, square footage, or cooling specification for this Hilliard building. AWS treats individual data center specifications as confidential and discloses capacity only at regional aggregate level. This facility sits within the AWS us-east-2 (Ohio) region and belongs to a three-campus cluster AWS has assembled in Hilliard since the mid-2010s, but the published record does not establish which campus the Britton Parkway address occupies or how much power it consumes.

The grid constraint is visible in the local framing of this buildout. To serve the newest Hilliard campus on Scioto Darby Road, AEP Ohio proposed a 228-cell, six-acre fuel cell installation as interim power ahead of new transmission capacity. The Ohio Power Siting Board approved the fuel cell plan in September and the Ohio EPA issued an air permit in October, over Hilliard city objections that state permitting pre-empted local review. Residents raised concerns about estimated one million pounds of daily carbon dioxide emissions from the installation and challenged the safety of the technology at this scale. The pattern shows hyperscale operators disclosing enormous capital commitments at campus scale while publishing no building-level technical specifications, leaving utility filings and permitting disputes as the main public window into actual buildout.

In Ohio, this registry maps 76 facilities and has read published megawatt figures from only 8 of them, totaling 60.4 MW across the state. This specific Hilliard building contributes no published figure and ranks ninth by capacity among Ohio facilities with published specifications, meaning it falls in a group whose power consumption remains undisclosed. The three-campus Hilliard cluster represents the largest disclosed AWS buildout in the state outside published capacity claims, anchoring a regional compute investment whose grid and fuel cell implications are now visible in state permitting records rather than operator spec sheets.
